results.title: Chicago Streets Etymology
results.description:
Numbered Streets on Chicago's South Side

Numbered streets are not drawn in this map for two reasons: because they would clutter the map, making it more difficult to navigate with a mouse, and because their collective history can be summed up here.   

In about 1861 officials determined that the street naming system in Chicago was too confusing; it was, and would continue to be for nearly another 50 years until 1909 when many of the streets in Chicago were renamed with a more organized system. They decided to replace the names on Chicago's South side with numbers. This was done for the benefit of commuters and tourists, making the city more easy to navigate. They apparently chose to number the South side streets because they believed those names were less sentimental than the street names on the North side, and because at the time Chicago was expanding southward and they expected it to continue to expand southward - this new and simple system would grow with the city. That was their plan anyways. We don't know why they didn't assign numbers to streets across the entire city.

Suffixes

Avenue - Title applied mostly to streets running North and South. There are exceptions. 
Blvd - Title given to streets where trucks over 5 tons are not permitted. 
Court - Title given to short roadway. 
Parkway - Title given to street that ends at a park. 
Place - Title given to street running the 1/2 block between streets. 
Street - Title applied mostly to streets running East and West. There are exceptions.

Data and Sources

The data for etymology came primarily from the publication "Chicago Streets" provided by the Chicago History Museum. I then turned to  Streetwise Chicago by authors Don Hayner and Tom McNamee for any entries that did not have histories in "Chicago Streets." Each historical blurb is a direct quote from either of these two sources. 

The Suffix data also comes from "Chicago Streets."

The Street Center Lines shapefile and Street Names table come from the Chicago Data Portal.

Information about the history of numbered streets on Chicago's South side came from Carrie Shepherd's article and podcast "Why some Chicago streets got numbers, others were stuck with names" published by WBEZ and Curious City.

results.title: Gaps in Spokane's Housing Crisis
results.description:
• SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition:
    • Website: https://www.selahnhc.org/about-selah
    • This organization's main goal is "responding to homelessness in a proactive, compassionate, and effective way" (SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, 2022). The organization does this by connecting those experiencing homelessness to local programs and resources; while prioritizing relationships on a local level instead of a broad level. The organization seems to help the local community, for example they raised $570,203 for their cause in 2022 (SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition, 2022). Their success seems to be in the way they focus on the community first before tackling more.
  • National Alliance to End Homelessness(NAEH)
    • Website: https://endhomelessness.org/
    • The NAEH works on three levels to end homelessness: creating policies, researching, and working to prioritize capacity-building (National Alliance to End Homelessness, 2024). The organization has been able to create change on a federal level because of the large size of the organization.
  • Ruff Institute of Global Homelessness
    • Website: https://ighomelessness.org/
    • On a global level, this organization works to end homelessness by prioritizing advocation, partnering with others to create solutions, and shedding light on homelessness (Ruff Institute of Global Homelessness, 2017). The global impact can definitely bee seen, but in a way it seems the project may be too large to actually see the progress it has made.
  • StreetWise
    • Website: https://www.streetwise.org/
    • StreetWise helps those that are experiencing homelessness by giving them employment. Their motto is, "a hand up, not a handout" (StreetWise, 2024). The program has existed since 1992 and has helped 500 people find employment (StreetWise, 2024). The level on which they interact with those in the community seems to be the biggest factor in their success.

results.name: SWB_Assets
results.title: Sewer and Water Board Asset Layers
results.description:
Overview

This feature service provides a collection of Sewerage and Water Board asset layers for the City of New Orleans. It brings together point, line, and polygon features that document major utility and drainage infrastructure, along with supporting attributes for location, ownership, status, construction details, and operational characteristics.

Feature Layers
  • Water Tanks — Point features representing water tank assets, including tank name, capacity, dimensions, water levels, zoning, service area, ownership, and source information.
  • Facilities — Point features for Sewerage and Water Board facilities with basic site information such as name, address, type, and comments.
  • Sewer Treatment Plants — Point features describing treatment plant assets and related site details such as basin, district, capacity, elevations, contact information, and operating status.
  • Sewer Pump Stations — Point features for sewer pump station assets with station identification, pump count, capacity, elevations, and location details.
  • Drainage Pump Stations — Point features representing drainage pump stations with structure characteristics, elevations, reconstruction information, and site contact or location details.
  • Force Mains — Line features representing force main infrastructure, with attributes for ownership, status, service area, basin, route, and length.
  • Sewer Lines — Line features representing sewer pipes and related network segments, including pipe structure, dimensions, upstream and downstream connections, material, status, basin, and route information.
  • Canals — Polygon features representing canal assets with canal identification, category, dimensions, ownership, status, service area, district, basin, and related descriptive information.
Geographic Coverage

The service covers the City of New Orleans and reflects Sewerage and Water Board infrastructure within the municipal service area.

Source and Vintage

The layers are sourced from the Sewerage and Water Board and reflect an event-era asset inventory associated with the August 5, 2017 flooding event. The service is presented as a static reference dataset.

Use Cases
  • Utility infrastructure inventory and reference
  • Drainage and wastewater system planning
  • Operational review of treatment, pumping, and conveyance assets
  • Map display and asset location lookup in GIS applications
Licensing

City of New Orleans license terms and disclaimer language apply to use of this service.

results.title: New Orleans Floods
results.description:
This paper seeks to show how climate change is increasing the intensity of flooding events and how the disasters associated with them fall most heavily on the most vulnerable levels of society. The case examined in this paper is that of Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans, where environmental forces, historical inequalities in housing, and inadequate infrastructure together created a crisis in which minority communities and low-income residents suffered from some of the worst and longest-lasting impacts.

While floods and hurricanes kill hundreds of thousands of people around the world every year, their impacts will continue not to be equally felt. Those already marginalized by poverty, race, disability, or lack of resources are invariably the ones paying the greatest price when disaster strikes.
results.snippet: An analysis of floods and the vulnerable people affected by them.

results.title: Flood Risk & Community Vulnerability in Orleans Parish, LA
results.description:
New Orleans is one of the most studied cities in the context of flood risk, and for good reason. Situated within the Mississippi River Delta, much of Orleans Parish sits at or below sea level, making it uniquely and persistently vulnerable to flooding from storm surge, heavy rainfall events, and the long-term effects of land subsidence. The devastation of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 brought these vulnerabilities into sharp national focus, yet the underlying conditions that made that disaster so catastrophic remain largely intact.

Understanding flood risk in a place like New Orleans requires looking beyond simple hazard mapping. Where water is likely to go tells only part of the story. Equally important is understanding who lives in those areas, what critical services and infrastructure are at stake, and which communities have the least capacity to prepare for, respond to, and recover from flood events. Flood risk, in other words, is as much a social phenomenon as it is a physical one.
results.snippet: A spatial analysis of physical flood susceptibility, critical infrastructure exposure, and social vulnerability

results.title: Recommendations for Accessible Risk Communication
results.description:
To better understand how New Orleans residents access and use flood emergency information, we conducted surveys and focus groups with residents across the city, including flood-prone neighborhoods such as the Lower 9th Ward, Hollygrove-Dixon, and New Orleans East in partnership with Emergency Legal Responders.

Three key findings emerged among residents in more flood-vulnerable communities:

  1. Trust shapes which information people use. Residents from historically marginalized communities were more likely to rely on information from trusted people and organizations than official sources for flood information compared to the broader population.
  2. Residents want neighborhood-specific information. Participants consistently expressed a need for place-based updates that reflected conditions in their own neighborhood, particularly during rapidly changing flash flood events.
  3. Risk information and protective actions are not well aligned. Residents often received alerts about hazardous conditions but little guidance on what actions they should take to protect themselves, their families, or their property.
results.snippet: A study creating community-centered flood risk information solutions for New Orleans.

results.title: Sustainability in New Orleans
results.description:
I chose New Orleans as my city for this assignment because I recently traveled there on an Alternative Break Trip with the MLD. This trip was a service learning trip and one of the civic highlights we focused on was environmental sustainability. New Orleans faces many sustainability challenges such as flooding and water management, climate change and resilience, environmental justice, energy use and efficiency, and waste management. I will focus on their flooding and water management issues.

By 2045, New Orleans faces significant challenges in flood protection and water management due to climate change, subsidence, and urban development. However, ongoing infrastructure improvements and resilience strategies aim to enhance the city's preparedness for future flooding events.​

results.title: FLOOD RISK AND SUSCEPTIBILITY MODELLING IN NEW ORLEANS EAST.
results.description: Flooding refers to the inundation of land while flood risk refers to the likelihood of a flooding event to occur in a particular area. Flood susceptibility however examines the vulnerability of an area to flooding and takes into consideration the social aspect such as humans (Parker 2014).
results.snippet: Alycia Prince-  816019033       Kristal Anchortassoo- 816020443

results.title: Coastal Inundation in Louisiana
results.description:
As climate change causes average ocean temperatures to increase, local sea-levels will rise and storms will be more common and more severe, threatening coastal communities.1  Proper mitigation of these storm surge events is essential to protect coastal communities before large storm events occur. Communities in Orleans Parish, Louisiana are increasingly at-risk for displacement from disaster events such as Hurricane Katrina which devastated New Orleans in 2005. Orleans Parish is especially vulnerable to flooding events due to its adjacency to the coast, large variations in at-risk populations, high percentage of impervious surfaces, and proximity to pollutants emitted from industrial plants in Cancer Alley.

Vulnerability is an intersectional issue that can reflect spatial patterns, so we employed both a suitability and overlay analysis with the above parameters to determine the most vulnerable communities in the Orleans Parish of Louisiana, USA in 2020. Repeating these analyses with census data from 1990 allows us to assess how vulnerability in Orleans Parish has changed over time, the results of which are used to spatially identify potential gaps in disaster response plans by showing the relationship between current evacuation routes and vulnerable communities.
results.snippet: A spatial analysis of populations vulnerable to coastal inundation in Orleans Parish.

results.title: Rising Tides, Hidden Vulnerabilities
results.description:
With rising sea levels, increased flood risk and the potential for mass migration from coastal locations have become more prevalent in the media. From articles revealing the extent of disappearing island communities, to articles covering the damage from hurricanes in the US south, flooding and flood risk have increased in many coastal communities as sea levels steadily rise. The city of New Orleans provides insights into the distribution of vulnerable communities and increased flood risk as a result of rising sea levels and overall climate change.

The New Orleans metropolitan area has an estimated population of over 1.2 million people, with its highest point of elevation reaching around 20 ft, and its lowest point rests at around 8 feet below sea level. In fact, more than half of the city is below sea level. From 1997 to 2019, the city experienced 69 flooding events, from coastal floods to storm surges and flash floods, exemplifying the city's need for adequate levee systems.
results.snippet: Mapping Flood Risk in New Orleans' Marginalized Communities

results.title: Effects of Hurricane Katrina
results.description:
The effects of Hurricane Katrina were seen throughout the whole nation. Communities were ripped apart, lives were lost, and infrastructure was destroyed. Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama are still in a constant state of rebuilding and planning for the next possible storm. The parish of New Orleans, one of the most affected areas, has implemented an advanced Hazard Mitigation Plan for every district to better protect the area and the communities within it.   

On August 23rd, 2005, a tropical depression skimmed over the Bahamas, approximately 350 miles east of Miami. Over the next two days, the storm began to grow stronger and earned the label of Tropical Storm Katriana and touched down as a category 1 hurricane between Miami and Fort Lauderdale, Florida with winds of 74-95 miles per hour.
results.snippet: LAND 4360 | Analyzing a Past Flood Event

results.title: Climate Change and Rising Sea Levels
results.description:
Sea Level Changes:

Over the last 100 years, global sea levels have risen by approximately 8-9 inches with an accelerated rate in the past few decades. NASA’s datasets show clear trends of rising sea levels, indicating that this issue will continue to worsen unless drastic action is taken. The projections for 2100 estimate an increase between 1 to 8 feet, depending on greenhouse gas emissions.

Key insight -
The data visualization highlights coastal areas most vulnerable to future sea level rise, including major metropolitan areas such as New York, Miami, and New Orleans, where flooding events are already becoming more frequent.
results.snippet: The impact that sea level and climate change have on coastal regions, and adaptation strategies cities can implement to help.

results.title: Flooding and Sea Level Rise in Coastal Communities
results.description:
Flooding as an Environmental Justice Issue

Sea level rise and coastal flooding are often discussed as environmental consequences of climate change, but their impacts are not experienced equally across societies. As oceans warm and expand, sea levels gradually rise, increasing the frequency and severity of coastal flooding, erosion, and saltwater intrusion. These physical changes threaten housing, infrastructure, drinking water systems, and local economies in coastal regions around the world. Scientific assessments show that rising seas are already increasing the probability of extreme flooding events and will continue to do so throughout this century (IPCC, 2022).

However, the consequences of sea level rise extend beyond environmental change. Flooding becomes an environmental justice issue when its impacts are shaped by social inequality. Communities with fewer economic resources, limited political power, or histories of discrimination often live in the most vulnerable coastal locations. Because of these structural conditions, they are more likely to experience repeated flooding, slower disaster recovery, and fewer opportunities for relocation or protection. In many cases, environmental hazards reinforce existing social inequities rather than affecting all populations equally (Elliott & Pais, 2006). Examining flooding through an environmental justice perspective helps reveal how climate risks intersect with differences in wealth, race, political power, and geographic location.
results.snippet: An environmental justice story about how sea level rise and coastal flooding disproportionately affect vulnerable communities in New Orleans

results.title: Drowning Cities: The Race Against Rising Seas
results.description:
Climate change is no longer a distant threat. It is reshaping our world today, particularly in America’s coastal cities. From Miami to New York, rising sea levels and increasingly intense storms are flooding streets, displacing residents, and jeopardizing local economies. These challenges highlight the urgent need for innovative solutions to protect our communities and ensure resilience in the face of environmental changes.

The Reality Of Rising Seas

Recent catastrophic hurricanes, such as Ian and Idalia, have devastated coastal communities, bringing the issue of urban resilience to the forefront. In cities like Miami, Charleston, and New Orleans, coastal flooding has become a regular event—even on sunny days. With billions of dollars in infrastructure and property at risk, and millions of lives affected, these challenges demand immediate action.

results.description:
This layer compiles the results of the natural hazards exposure analysis for defined community areas across Otago, as as per the report in progress ‘Otago region natural hazards exposure analysis (ORC, 2025).


 

Community area boundaries for urban areas and rural settlements, and other rural areas outside of these settlements are defined by Stats NZ (2022) statistical area geographies SA1 and SA2. They reflect communities that interact socially and economically. In urban areas, they are equivalent to suburbs. Please refer to pages xx in the source report for more information on the geography datasets used in the analysis.


 

Communities that have a comparatively higher amount of vital elements (e.g. buildings, critical community facilities, population) intersecting a mapped natural hazard area are classified with a higher level of exposure; and those with a lower amount are classified with a comparatively lower level of exposure.


 

Please refer to the source report for specific information on how exposure (pgs 9-11) is determined for community areas across Otago and for more detailed information on the methodology used in the analysis.

results.description:
This dataset comes from the FEMA S_Fld_Haz_Ar table. The S_Fld_Haz_Ar table contains information about the flood hazards within the flood risk project area. A spatial file with location information also corresponds with this data table. These zones are used by FEMA to designate the SFHA and for insurance rating purposes. These data are the regulatory flood zones designated by FEMA. A spatial file with location information also corresponds with this data table.
    This information is needed for the following tables in the FIS report: Flooding Sources Included in this FIS report, and Summary of Hydrologic and Hydraulic Analyses.
      The spatial elements representing the flood zones are polygons. The entire area of the jurisdiction(s) mapped by the FIRM should have a corresponding flood zone polygon. There is one polygon for each contiguous flood zone designated.
      • FEMA Regulatory Floodway are flood zone polygons marked as a regulatory floodway.
      • FEMA 100 year are flood zone polygons where there is a 1% Annual Chance, also known as the 100 year.
      • FEMA 500 year are flood zone polygons where there is a 0.2% Annual Chance, also known as the 500 year.
      • FEMA minimal flood hazard zone polygons.
      This map is not intended for insurance rating purposes and is for information only. This map is a representation and approximation of the relative location of geographic information, land marks and physical addresses. The map may not be 100% accurate in locating your address. The floodplains shown on this mapping tool are those delineated on the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (FEMA) Digital Flood Insurance Rate Map (DFIRM or floodplain map) for Montgomery County. This map is not an official FEMA Digital Flood Insurance Rate Map. The effective DFIRMs are produced, maintained, and published by FEMA and not by Montgomery County. Official determinations are provided by FEMA.

results.description:
EUC All Data by Census Tract (w/ Additional Flood Plain & Public Health Data)

Location: Rhode Island

Description:
Shapefile containing data from the four factors (% vacant, % industrial, % green, & SVI) relevant for green infrastructure analysis for SRC EUC-17, with additional Flood Plain and Public Health data included. Data is organized by US Census tract, and includes GEOID (2016 US Census tract identifier). File combines and simplifies multiple layers, described in detail below:
  • Site Boundary - Simple shapefile delineating the border of the three study areas.
  • Census Tracts - Shapefile delineating 2016 US Census tracts and related data.

results.title: City of Beatrice, NE Flood Loss Analysis All Property Data
results.description:
Following a historic flood in 1973, Beatrice decided to begin purchasing flood-prone properties instead of rebuilding. From 1977 to 2014, Beatrice bought 120 properties with a total investment of $4.9 million. Beatrice converted the purchased properties into parks, open space, ball fields, hiking and biking trails, and other outdoor uses.

On May 7th, 2015, the Big Blue River rose to its third highest crest and officials saw firsthand the benefits of the flood mitigation strategy implemented in the City. The City of Beatrice, NE Official Mitigation Effectiveness Story Map tells the story of the mitigation effectiveness study that followed the event in an effort to quantify the benefits and demonstrate the value of this type of mitigation for other communities.

The City of Beatrice, NE All Loss Properties were used as reference during the analysis and they are also used as reference in the storymap shortlist embedded in Tab 3 "A Mitigation Success Story" of the City of Beatrice, NE Official Mitigation Effectiveness Story Map.

results.name: Recorded_Floodplain_Easements
results.title: Recorded Floodplain Easements
results.description: Floodplain delineations were first added to the County tax maps in the 1970's for creeks and streams with watersheds of 1 square mile or greater. In 1977 all the studies on these large streams had been completed and a "Floodplain Overlay District" was created. Within several years this floodplain overlay district was depicted on the zoning maps. Again, these delineations were only for those creeks with drainage areas of over 1 square mile. A note in a 1981 memo to the Mapping Division about these delineations said, "...the County delineation of a Flood Plain Overlay District line on the tax map is treated here as a flag or general indicator of approximate location of this District's line. Normal development provides 2 field run topography professionally certified on which the floodplain elevations can be more accurately determined..." In 1985 the Zoning Ordinance was amended, an entire section on floodplains was added to Chapter 2 and the definition of what constituted a floodplain was significantly revised. Where as the Floodplain Overlay District had principally contained only those overbank areas inundated by the 100-yr storm along streams with drainage areas of 1 square mile or greater (i.e. 640 acres), the new definition included the overbank areas inundated by the 100-year storm along creeks with drainage areas of 70 acres and greater. But this change in the definition of floodplain created a problem for those who had become dependent on the tax maps to show them whether or not there was floodplain on a given property. These newly-defined floodplains were not yet studied or mapped and would only be mapped one property at a time, as each parcel containing these smaller floodplains submitted plans for development. When such parcels were developed, floodplain studies were required, and floodplain easements (later titled "floodplain and storm drainage easements") were recorded around these smaller floodplains. And as those easements were recorded, they were added to the tax maps. For all the floodplains which have been studied since 1985, the limits of the floodplain and storm drainage easements have been added to the tax maps, when such easements were required by the County Code or the Zoning Ordinance. But if a parcel has not yet been developed or if it was developed prior to 1985, there is usually no easement around the floodplain. There are also numerous cases where, for some reason, floodplain easements were recorded along small creeks with drainage areas well below 70 acres. These recorded "floodplain" easements were then added to the tax maps. THE RESULT: The tax maps cannot be used to definitively determine whether floodplain exists on a given parcel .There are approximately 900 miles of streams which meet the 70 acre drainage area requirement for floodplains, but to date (6/2003) almost 400 of these 900 miles remain unstudied. And if a stream has never been studied, no easement would have been recorded and thus the fact that it was a floodplain would not be reflected in the tax maps. Only after a determination of the drainage area is made can one know whether the overbank areas along a given creek meet the Zoning Ordinance definition of floodplain. Further if the drainage area is over 70 acres, only a floodplain study can determine the limits of the floodplain that is, how much of the overbank areas are inundated by the peak flow of the 100-yr storm. The layer for floodplains with drainage areas of over 1 square mile is good, but above that, it's inconsistent, especially in those areas which are minor floodplains (i.e. less than 360 acres of drainage area) and which were developed prior to 1985. The entire 850 or so miles of floodplain have not been mapped as unbroken corridors. And the "floodplain" here in Fairfax County, we're using the zoning ordinance definition which is the 100-yr water surface limits along streams with drainage areas of over 70 acres. This definition came into the zoning ordinance in 1985, so from that time, developers have had to study and map even these smaller floodplains on their developments and put them in easements. These easements have been captured on our tax maps since 1985, development by development, as the record plats were recorded. FEMA doesn't recognize as Special Flood Hazard Areas, many stream valleys that we would call floodplain. The layer currently on the data loader for floodplains is missing many segments of stream that are defined as floodplain per the zoning ordinance. results.name: WaterbodyExtractionSAR_USA.dlpk
results.title: Water Body Extraction (SAR) - USA
results.description:
Water is an indispensable resource not only for humans but for all living being on earth. Conservation and management of water resources helps sustain and thrive life and also prevent its destruction. Water management can include activities such as monitoring the changing course of rivers and streams, regional planning, flood management, agriculture, and so on, all of which requires survey and planning, including accurate mapping of water bodies. Hence, extraction of water bodies from remote sensing data is critical to record how this dynamic changes and map their current forms. The remote sensing data used here is SAR, which is a powerful imagery for information extraction, as it is unaffected by cloud cover, acquires images overnight, enables all-weather imaging, and it is cost effective compared to other imageries. This deep learning model can be used to automate the task of extracting water bodies from SAR imagery.

Using the model

Follow the guide to use the model. Before using this model, ensure that the supported deep learning libraries are installed. For more details, check Deep Learning Libraries Installer for ArcGIS.


Fine-tuning the model
This model can be fine-tuned using the Train Deep Learning Model tool. Follow the guide to fine-tune this model.

Input
8-bit, 3-band Sentinel-1 C band SAR GRD VH polarization band raster.

Output
Binary raster representing water and non-water classes

Applicable geographies
The model is expected to work well in the United States.

Model architecture
The model uses the DeepLab model architecture implemented in ArcGIS API for Python.

Accuracy metrics
The model has a precision of 0.945, recall of 0.92 and F1-score of 0.933.

Training data
This model is trained on manually classified training dataset. Labels were created by using Sentinel-1 C band SAR GRD VH polarization imagery using histogram based thresholding method, followed by QA and manual cleaning to get water masks.

Sample results
Here are few results from the model.
results.snippet: Deep learning model to extract and map water bodies from Sentinel-1 SAR imagery, enabling accurate detection under all-weather and cloud-free conditions. This model supports water resource management, flood monitoring, and environmental analysis by automatically identifying water features across large geographic regions.

The National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) data incorporates all Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases published by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and any Letters of Map Revision (LOMRs) that have been issued against those databases since their publication date. It is updated on a monthly basis. The FIRM Database is the digital, geospatial version of the flood hazard information shown on the published paper FIRMs. The FIRM Database depicts flood risk information and supporting data used to develop the risk data. The primary risk classifications used are the 1-percent-annual-chance flood event, the 0.2-percent-annual-chance flood event, and areas of minimal flood risk. The FIRM Database is derived from Flood Insurance Studies (FISs), previously published FIRMs, flood hazard analyses performed in support of the FISs and FIRMs, and new mapping data, where available. The FISs and FIRMs are published by FEMA. The NFHL is available as State or US Territory data sets. Each State or Territory data set consists of all FIRM Databases and corresponding LOMRs available on the publication date of the data set. The specification for the horizontal control of FIRM Databases is consistent with those required for mapping at a scale of 1:12,000. This file is georeferenced to the Earth's surface using the Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) and North American Datum of 1983.

This data reflects the changes FEMA is proposing for the Thurston County DFIRM (Digital Flood Insurance Rate Maps) base elevation adjustment. The floodzone boundaries have been adjusted to match the new base flood elevation standard. This change involved transforming the BFE from NAD 27 to NAD 83, which resulted a a shift of several feet.

** FEMA defines Floodway as "A "Regulatory Floodway" means the channel of a river or other watercourse and the adjacent land areas that must be reserved in order to discharge the base flood without cumulatively increasing the water surface elevation more than a designated height."

The FIRM is the basis for floodplain management, mitigation, and insurance activities for the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). Insurance applications include enforcement of the mandatory purchase requirement of the Flood Disaster Protection Act, which "... requires the purchase of flood insurance by property owners who are being assisted by Federal programs or by Federally supervised, regulated or insured agencies or institutions in the acquisition or improvement of land facilities located or to be located in identified areas having special flood hazards, " Section 2 (b) (4) of the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973. In addition to the identification of Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), the risk zones shown on the FIRMs are the basis for the establishment of premium rates for flood coverage offered through the NFIP. The FIRM Database presents the flood risk information depicted on the FIRM in a digital format suitable for use in electronic mapping applications. The FIRM Database serves to archive the information collected during the Flood Risk Project.

results.description:
Overview

This map service presents aerial orthophotography and the City Boundary for the City of Kelowna.

Layers

  • Orthophoto imagery representing high-resolution aerial photo coverage for 2017.
  • City Boundary represented as a polygon layer showing the municipal boundary.

Characteristics

The service combines a detailed image base with a polygon boundary layer. The imagery provides visual context for buildings, roads, land use, and surface features, while the boundary layer identifies the municipal extent.

Image interpretation: The orthophoto layer is a continuous aerial image surface, with each pixel carrying color information from the 2017 flight imagery. It is suitable for visual interpretation, base mapping, and spatial comparison.

Geographic Coverage

The service covers the City of Kelowna,  UTM Zone 11, with a municipal-scale extent centered on the urban area and surrounding boundary.

Use Cases

This service is useful for municipal mapping, visual inspection of current landscape conditions, boundary reference, and general geographic analysis within Kelowna.

NOTE: 

Kelowna 2017 Ortho imagery was flown  on Sunday May 21, 2017  this was during the  2017 Freshet Flooding Event. The lake level on that day was 342.8m.
Please note that not all flood mitigation measures were in place at the time the imagery was flown.

results.title: D5_2030_Hatch
results.description:
Flood Hatch Shapefiles
In addition to the three sets of rasters (Maximum Wave Heights, Water Surface Elevations, and DFEs) provided, separate shapefiles were also created to overlap and highlight special areas within the raster datasets produced for calculating DFEs. A flood hatch shapefile is not provided for every ACFEP level or for every region, but when it is provided, it encompasses the special areas for that level and region. The same hatch shapefile is applicable for all datatypes for the particular level and region. Flood hatch shapefiles encompass all areas of special values within the data rasters (including areas of 9999, 9998, and 9997 values). All regions have a 0.1% ACFEP level flood hatch shapefile because all 0.1% ACFEP rasters contain 9999 values.
The flood hatch shapefiles contain individual polygons that describe the type of special area underlying that polygon’s spatial extent. For 9999 and 9998 values in the value rasters (water surface elevations, waves, and DFEs), the special hatched polygons will have the same extent of those values within those rasters. For 9997 values in the value rasters, the hatch polygon will always encompass the 9997 values, but may be larger in extent than just the location of those value cells. For these areas, water surface elevation, wave heights, and DFEs values may be provided, but they still represent a special zone.
The Hatch polygons have 5 fields (Column headers) that describe each polygon within the shapefile. These fields include FID, Shape, Hatch_Type, Zones_txt, Hatch, and Hatch_Txt. The FID field contains an ID number for each polygon within that shapefile, while the Shape field
lists the type of shapefile contained (polygon in all cases). The Hatch_Type field contains the numerical value that can be found within the value rasters (wave height, water surface, and DFE) underlying that polygon. Zones_txt and Hatch_txt are string type fields that contain descriptors of the polygon type, while the Hatch Field contains a numerical value for the type of hatching (1 for 0.1% Edge Zone, 2 for Wave Overtopping Zones, 3 for Dynamic Zone). The following table is an example of what a flood hatch file’s attribute table might look like.
FID
Shape
Hatch_Type
Zones_Txt
Hatch
Hatch_Txt
0
Polygon
9999
Shallow water flooding during extreme storms
1
0.1% Edge Zone
1
Polygon
9997
Influenced by wave overtopping (incl. 9997 areas)

Wave Overtopping Zone

Polygon
9998

Specifically, the various hatch shapefiles can be defined as follows:
• FID 0 Hatch Type – These represent areas of shallow water flooding during extreme storms. These are locations where flooding can only be expected during the most extreme events (> 1000-year return period) or where there are only minor flood depths (shallow flooding) during 1000-year return period AEP. These values only appear in 0.1% ACFEP level since they only occur at the very upper extent of extreme flooding. Water surface elevation values in these regions can be set to 0.1 foot above the site-specific land elevation to provide an estimate of the water surface elevation. Site-specific survey information may be needed to determine the land elevation. These hatch areas directly match areas with 9999 values within the rasters.
• FID 1 Hatch Type – These represent wave overtopping zones. These hatch layers encompass the 9997 areas, but also include areas that have known values. Hatched areas of this type covering 9997 values would be expected to experience flooding caused by intermittent wave spray and overtopping only. Hatched areas of this type covering locations with values indicate that the flooding is caused by both direct sheet flow and wave overtopping. These hatched zones are provided for informational purposes by identifying zones that may require special design considerations for wave overtopping. results.title: Southeastern Kentucky Special Flood Hazard Zone Information
results.description:
A layer made from a feature service published on EEC's Watermaps server. This layer displays Special Flood Hazard Area information for the region of Southeastern Kentucky that was affected by the flooding events that happened in the summer of 2022. All 100 Year Floodplain areas are viewable at 1:100,000 scale and all Cross Sections are viewable at 1:50,000, this was a decision made to improve performance of the service. The data originates from a collaboration of AECOM and Stantec.

Flood hazard areas identified on the Flood Insurance Rate Map are identified as a Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA). SFHA are defined as the area that will be inundated by the flood event having a 1-percent chance of being equaled or exceeded in any given year. The 1-percent annual chance flood is also referred to as the base flood or 100-year flood. - From the FEMA Glossary

results.name: survey123_10e43f3cd8314ed68de7802797c72a2a
results.title: Eligibility Selection Survey
results.description:
This dataset contains all residential properties located within designated urban areas of California that meet the eligibility criteria established under Senate Bill 9 (SB 9). It includes parcels that satisfy key requirements such as zoning, lot size, and access conditions, and excludes properties restricted by factors like historic designation, high fire hazard severity zones, flood zones, or environmentally sensitive areas where SB 9 does not apply.

The dataset is intended to support planners, developers, researchers, and property owners in identifying parcels that are legally eligible for lot splits and/or duplex development under SB 9, helping to streamline analysis, feasibility studies, and housing development planning across California’s urban regions.
results.snippet:
This dataset includes all properties with valid Assessor’s Parcel Numbers (APNs) that have been selected through a structured screening process and determined to qualify for development under California Senate Bill 9 (SB 9).

All listed properties have been evaluated against the required SB 9 eligibility standards, including zoning and land-use designation, minimum lot size, access and frontage conditions, and the absence of disqualifying constraints such as historic status, high fire hazard severity zones, flood risk areas, or protected environmental lands. In addition, each property has been accurately analyzed using the 40–60% development criteria, ensuring that the proposed lot split or duplex configuration meets the proportional size and usability requirements set by SB 9 guidelines.

Only parcels that successfully passed both the 40–60% rule and all other applicable SB 9 criteria are included, making this dataset a refined list of properties with high potential for SB 9–compliant development, suitable for planning analysis, feasibility studies, and housing opportunity assessments.

results.name: HighGroundwaterHazardAreas
results.title: HighGroundwaterHazardAreas
results.description:
Last Updated on 9/7/2021 by SLS.

The purpose of this data is to provide planners with a history of flooding events recorded in the county. This information is compiled using authoritative data and represents the approximate mapped location of documented high groundwater flooding events for the purposes of screening. Authoritative data includes, but is not limited to, the 1997 WA State DOT infrared aerial photography.

Beginning in 2016 updates to this layer began, and are in progress, to eliminate shadowing and map high groundwater using digital versions of the 1997 Aerial Photography (not available when the layer was first created) and LiDAR Contour data. All edits are verified by the County Hydrogeologist and Flood Plain Manager before being incorporated into the data. Edits are made on a case-by-case basis as time allows and when discrepancies are found and researched.

For information about changes or making a change please contact Tim Rubert, Flood Plain Manager, with Thurston County.

High ground water hazard areas as defined in the Thurston County Critical Areas Ordinance Chapter 24.20, adopted on July 24, 2012 Or No 14773.

24.20.015 High ground water flood hazard areas – Base flood elevation.

The base flood elevation (BFE) for high ground water flood hazard areas corresponds to the elevation of the outer edge of the high ground water flood hazard area. The map entitled “High Ground Water Flood Hazard Areas,” depicts the approximate location of the high groundwater flood hazard area. The actual location of the outer edge of the flood hazard area shall be determined consistent with TCC 24.20.030 and 24.20.035, as applicable.

For these requested outputs, Woods Hole Group created a set of geographic data features and raster datasets. These datasets were calculated directly from the MC-FRM model simulation results but required additional calculation and processing efforts to create the required GIS based outputs. ABSTRACT
The National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) data incorporates all Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases published by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), and any Letters of Map Revision (LOMRs) that have been issued against those databases since their publication date. It is updated on a monthly basis. The FIRM Database is the digital, geospatial version of the flood hazard information shown on the published paper FIRMs.  

The FIRM Database depicts flood risk information and supporting data used to develop the risk data. The primary risk classifications used are the 1-percent-annual-chance flood event, the 0.2-percent-annual-chance flood event, and areas of minimal flood risk. The FIRM Database is derived from Flood Insurance Studies (FISs), previously published FIRMs, flood hazard analyses performed in support of the FISs and FIRMs, and new mapping data, where available. The FISs and FIRMs are published by FEMA.

The NFHL is available as State or US Territory data sets.  Each State or Territory data set consists of all FIRM Databases and corresponding LOMRs available on the publication date of the data set. 

The specification for the horizontal control of FIRM Databases is consistent with those required for mapping at a scale of 1:12,000. This file is georeferenced to the Earth's surface using the Geographic Coordinate System (GCS) and North American Datum of 1983.

PURPOSE
The FIRM is the basis for floodplain management, mitigation, and insurance activities for the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). Insurance applications include enforcement of the mandatory purchase requirement of the Flood Disaster Protection Act, which "... requires the purchase of flood insurance by property owners who are being assisted by Federal programs or by Federally supervised, regulated or insured agencies or institutions in the acquisition or improvement of land facilities located or to be located in identified areas having special flood hazards, " Section 2 (b) (4) of the Flood Disaster Protection Act of 1973. In addition to the identification of Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs), the risk zones shown on the FIRMs are the basis for the establishment of premium rates for flood coverage offered through the NFIP. The FIRM Database presents the flood risk information depicted on the FIRM in a digital format suitable for use in electronic mapping applications. The FIRM Database  serves to archive the information collected during the Flood Risk Project.

results.name: SouthAL_Watersheds
results.title: SouthAL_Watersheds
results.description: The Watershed Boundary Dataset (WBD) is a comprehensive aggregated collection of hydrologic unit data consistent with the national criteria for delineation and resolution. It defines the areal extent of surface water drainage to a point except in coastal or lake front areas where there could be multiple outlets as stated by the "Federal Standards and Procedures for the National Watershed Boundary Dataset (WBD)" "Standard" (https://pubs.usgs.gov/tm/11/a3/). Watershed boundaries are determined solely upon science-based hydrologic principles, not favoring any administrative boundaries or special projects, nor particular program or agency. This dataset represents the hydrologic unit boundaries to the 12-digit (6th level) for the entire United States. Some areas may also include additional subdivisions representing the 14- and 16-digit hydrologic unit (HU). At a minimum, the HUs are delineated at 1:24,000-scale in the conterminous United States, 1:25,000-scale in Hawaii, Pacific basin and the Caribbean, and 1:63,360-scale in Alaska, meeting the National Map Accuracy Standards (NMAS). Higher resolution boundaries are being developed where partners and data exist and will be incorporated back into the WBD. WBD data are delivered as a dataset of polygons and corresponding lines that define the boundary of the polygon. WBD polygon attributes include hydrologic unit codes (HUC), size (in the form of acres and square kilometers), name, downstream hydrologic unit code, type of watershed, non-contributing areas, and flow modifications. The HUC describes where the unit is in the country and the level of the unit. WBD line attributes contain the highest level of hydrologic unit for each boundary, line source information and flow modifications. The intent of defining Hydrologic Units (HU) within the Watershed Boundary Dataset is to establish a base-line drainage boundary framework, accounting for all land and surface areas. Hydrologic units are intended to be used as a tool for water-resource management and planning activities particularly for site-specific and localized studies requiring a level of detail provided by large-scale map information. The WBD complements the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) and supports numerous programmatic missions and activities including: watershed management, rehabilitation and enhancement, aquatic species conservation strategies, flood plain management and flood prevention, water-quality initiatives and programs, dam safety programs, fire assessment and management, resource inventory and assessment, water data analysis and water census.</purpose><supplinf>The WBD was produced and is maintained through a cooperative process involving state, federal and local partners. Process information for a specific state or region can be found within the state specific metadata located at ftp://rockyftp.cr.usgs.gov/ngtoc/hydro/outgoing/WBDArchivedMetadata/. This metadata file has information for WBD features contained in the WBD feature dataset. This includes information about the 2-, 4-, 6-, 8-, 10-, 12-, 14-, 16-digit polygons and WBD_Line dataset. Users accessing the WBD via shapefile will need to search for the attribution related to that specific dataset.

results.title: Alberta Floods Portal
results.description:
Alberta Environment and Parks identifies flood-prone areas across the province as part of the Flood Hazard Identification Program. Flood studies are detailed assessments of flood risk along a specific river reaches. They include flood maps that identify where water will flow during a flood and what land could be flooded for different sized floods. Flood studies can include both open water and ice jam flood maps where appropriate. Flood hazard maps are typically used for long range planning, to inform land use decisions; and are available to all levels of government and the public to help build resilient communities.

Flood maps are created by combining hydraulic model results with high-accuracy ground information. Field surveys and LiDAR remote sensing are used to collect river and floodplain elevations, channel cross section data, bridge and culvert information, and flood berm details. A hydrology assessment using recorded and historic flow measurements is typically used to estimate river flows for a wide range of possible open water floods with different chances of occurring each year. When appropriate, an ice jam frequency analysis is undertaken. All this information is used to build a hydraulic model of a river system, which is calibrated using highwater marks and aerial imagery from past floods to ensure that results for the different flood flows being mapped are reasonable. Flood inundation maps show areas at risk for different sized floods, including ice jam floods in some communities. These maps also identify areas that could be flooded if berms or other flood control structures fail and are typically used for emergency response planning and to inform local infrastructure design. Flood hazards have not been identified along all rivers or through all communities, and it is important to remember that risk exists in areas without provincial flood maps.

results.description:
Last Updated on 9/7/2021 by SLS.

The purpose of this data is to provide planners with a history of flooding events recorded in the county. This information is compiled using authoritative data and represents the approximate mapped location of documented high groundwater flooding events for the purposes of screening. Authoritative data includes, but is not limited to, the 1997 WA State DOT infrared aerial photography.

Beginning in 2016 updates to this layer began, and are in progress, to eliminate shadowing and map high groundwater using digital versions of the 1997 Aerial Photography (not available when the layer was first created) and LiDAR Contour data. All edits are verified by the County Hydrogeologist and Flood Plain Manager before being incorporated into the data. Edits are made on a case-by-case basis as time allows and when discrepancies are found and researched.

For information about changes or making a change please contact Tim Rubert, Flood Plain Manager, with Thurston County.

High ground water hazard areas as defined in the Thurston County Critical Areas Ordinance Chapter 24.20, adopted on July 24, 2012 Or No 14773.

24.20.015 High ground water flood hazard areas – Base flood elevation.

The base flood elevation (BFE) for high ground water flood hazard areas corresponds to the elevation of the outer edge of the high ground water flood hazard area. The map entitled “High Ground Water Flood Hazard Areas,” depicts the approximate location of the high groundwater flood hazard area. The actual location of the outer edge of the flood hazard area shall be determined consistent with TCC 24.20.030 and 24.20.035, as applicable.

results.name: ReservoirFloodExtentsWetDay
results.title: Reservoir Flood Extents - Wet Day (National)
results.description:
This data shows the individual flood extents for all large raised reservoirs in the event that they were to fail and release the water held on a “wet day” when local rivers had already overflowed their banks. It represents a prediction of a credible worst case scenario, however it’s unlikely that any actual flood would be this large. The data gives no indication of likelihood or probability of reservoir flooding. Flood extents are not included for smaller reservoirs or for reservoirs commissioned after the reservoir modelling programme began in October 2016.

In 2010 the Environment Agency published the National Reservoir Inundation Maps. The maps provide an indication of the flooding that would occur if a failure of a reservoir embankment or structure led to an uncontrolled release of water. The Environment Agency has reviewed, updated and improved the reservoir flood maps as part of the Reservoir Flood Mapping Project. The maps show the extent of flooding for all large-raised reservoirs that were in operation in October 2016. New reservoirs after that date will be modelled under the next review of the flood maps, which is due in by 2025.

results.description: The Watershed Boundary Dataset (WBD) is a comprehensive aggregated collection of hydrologic unit data consistent with the national criteria for delineation and resolution. It defines the areal extent of surface water drainage to a point except in coastal or lake front areas where there could be multiple outlets as stated by the "Federal Standards and Procedures for the National Watershed Boundary Dataset (WBD)" "Standard" (https://pubs.usgs.gov/tm/11/a3/). Watershed boundaries are determined solely upon science-based hydrologic principles, not favoring any administrative boundaries or special projects, nor particular program or agency. This dataset represents the hydrologic unit boundaries to the 12-digit (6th level) for the entire United States. Some areas may also include additional subdivisions representing the 14- and 16-digit hydrologic unit (HU). At a minimum, the HUs are delineated at 1:24,000-scale in the conterminous United States, 1:25,000-scale in Hawaii, Pacific basin and the Caribbean, and 1:63,360-scale in Alaska, meeting the National Map Accuracy Standards (NMAS). Higher resolution boundaries are being developed where partners and data exist and will be incorporated back into the WBD. WBD data are delivered as a dataset of polygons and corresponding lines that define the boundary of the polygon. WBD polygon attributes include hydrologic unit codes (HUC), size (in the form of acres and square kilometers), name, downstream hydrologic unit code, type of watershed, non-contributing areas, and flow modifications. The HUC describes where the unit is in the country and the level of the unit. WBD line attributes contain the highest level of hydrologic unit for each boundary, line source information and flow modifications. The intent of defining Hydrologic Units (HU) within the Watershed Boundary Dataset is to establish a base-line drainage boundary framework, accounting for all land and surface areas. Hydrologic units are intended to be used as a tool for water-resource management and planning activities particularly for site-specific and localized studies requiring a level of detail provided by large-scale map information. The WBD complements the National Hydrography Dataset (NHD) and supports numerous programmatic missions and activities including: watershed management, rehabilitation and enhancement, aquatic species conservation strategies, flood plain management and flood prevention, water-quality initiatives and programs, dam safety programs, fire assessment and management, resource inventory and assessment, water data analysis and water census.</purpose><supplinf>The WBD was produced and is maintained through a cooperative process involving state, federal and local partners. Process information for a specific state or region can be found within the state specific metadata located at ftp://rockyftp.cr.usgs.gov/ngtoc/hydro/outgoing/WBDArchivedMetadata/. This metadata file has information for WBD features contained in the WBD feature dataset. This includes information about the 2-, 4-, 6-, 8-, 10-, 12-, 14-, 16-digit polygons and WBD_Line dataset. Users accessing the WBD via shapefile will need to search for the attribution related to that specific dataset.

results.title: First Street Foundation: Normalized Flood Risk - Census Tracts
results.description:
This dataset shows normalized flood risk for all census tracts within the contiguous United States, as based on the First Street Foundation Flood Model. The normalization process takes the percentage of properties within a tract with exposure to the 100-year flood, and transforms this number to a percentile (relative to all other census tracts).
 
First Street Foundation is a non-profit research and technology group defining America’s flood risk. Please let us know how your organization is using our publicly available data offered through ArcGIS Online (e.g. resiliency reports, adaptation studies, etc.). This helps inform what datasets we make publicly available in the future. Contact datashare@firststreet.org.
 
First Street Foundation is committed to the accuracy of the data and will continue to grow, adapt, and change the Flood Model with new and better information. As such, improvements to the Flood Model are incorporated in quarterly updates. The statistics presented here are consistent with First Street Foundation Flood Model version 1.3 released on May 7, 2021.
 
The aggregated data presented here are available from First Street Foundation at the individual property level. Please go to First Street’s Data Access page for more information.

Dataset Field Names

The following fields are included in this dataset:

Attribute

Description

FIPS

Census Tract FIPS Code

COUNTY

County

STATE

State

norm_2020

Normalized flood risk percentile for the year 2020. Based on percent of properties within the census tract with exposure to the 100 year flood in the medium climate scenario. Percentile relative to all other tracts in the contiguous United States.

norm_2050

Normalized flood risk percentile for the year 2050. Based on percent of properties within the census tract with exposure to the 100 year flood in the medium climate scenario. Percentile relative to all other tracts in the contiguous United States.

diff_2020_2050

Percentile difference between “norm_2020” and “norm_2050”. This number will be positive for tracts that are projected to increase in flood risk relative to other tracts over the next 30 years. This number will be negative for tracts that are projected to decrease in flood risk relative to other tracts over the next 30 years.


Normalization Method

The method used to normalize flood risk is based on a min-max scaling process that assigns a percentile to each census tract in the contiguous United States. The percentile is based on percent of properties within the tract with exposure to the 100 year flood in the medium climate scenario (the First Street Foundation Flood Model incorporates the output of an ensemble of 21 Global Climate Models to account for the uncertainty of future climate scenarios as well as the current climate itself).

The min-max scaling method results in a transformation to percentiles within a range of values that are restricted to the minimum and maximum values of the variable being scaled. The equation is (value - min) / (max - min), where each term represents the following:
  • value: the % of properties exposed to the hazard in each specific year
  • min: the minimum % of properties exposed to the hazard in each specific year
  • max: the maximum % of properties exposed to the hazard in each specific year
First Street Data Availability

The aggregated data presented here are available from First Street Foundation at the individual property level. Please go to First Street’s Data Access page for more information.

Data Credits
  • Normalized flood risk data by First Street Foundation
  • Census Tract boundaries by Esri

results.title: NY-NJ Advisory Base Flood Elevations (06/20/2013)
results.description:
FEMA, as the administrator of the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), has created Advisory Base Flood Elevations (ABFEs) to show a more current picture of flood risk for several communities in New Jersey and New York affected by Hurricane Sandy. The known flood risk has changed since the last effective community Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) as a result of the disaster, recent development in coastal and floodplain areas, or the availability of more current data. The ABFE information and related layers depicted on this web service for certain communities in New Jersey and New York can serve as a guide to understanding current coastal flood hazard conditions and higher elevations that communities should build to in order to reduce impacts of similar events in the future.  A complete listing of layers is provided below.  All elevations included on the map are referenced to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD 88).  






Additional information on ABFEs, including information on how they were developed and recommended uses is available through FEMA’s Region 2 Coastal Outreach website at www.region2coastal.com.

results.name: VashonMauryShorelineBuildings_area
results.title: VashonMauryShorelineBuildings_area
results.description:
This layer contains all buildings in the Coastal High Hazard Area (FEMA High Risk Flood Areas/100-yr Floodplain), Sea-Level Rise Risk Area, or 100 feet landward of the Sea-Level Rise Risk Area for Vashon-Maury Island. For the purposes of this layer, temporary structures or structures without walls (such as a carport) are not included.

Building outlines in the layer were first generated in 2012 as part of a flood study on Vashon-Maury Island using 2009 aerial imagery. These data were used as a starting point for the 2024-2025 effort. In the 2024-2025 effort, GIS analysts at King County reviewed all existing buildings, edited geometry and/or added buildings as necessary, and deleted buildings where there were bad digitizations. As a main purpose of this data is to track progress towards goals in the Clean Water Healthy Habitats (CWHH) initiative, buildings that were demolished are retained in this dataset and flagged as such. It is important to note that features in this dataset may be demolished buildings that do not exist anymore. Tracking these improvements relative the CWHH goals is a critical function of this dataset.

A number of attributes relevant to tracking expansion or contraction of development in the shoreline area are included in this data and described in attribute (fields) section of the metadata. For questions about the project and/or project goals, contact Kollin Higgins at kollin.higgings@kingcounty.gov.

More information about the CWHH initiative can be found here: https://kingcounty.gov/en/dept/dnrp/about-king-county/about-dnrp/sustainability-commitments/clean-water-healthy-habitat
results.snippet: This layer contains all buildings in the Coastal High Hazard Area (FEMA High Risk Flood Areas/100-yr Floodplain), Sea-Level Rise Risk Area, or 100 feet landward of the Sea-Level Rise Risk Area for Vashon-Maury Island. This layer is used for tracking development in the aforementioned hazard areas, as well as for tracking progress towards goals laid out in the Clean Water Healthy Habitats initiative. results.title: TRCA Regulation Limit
results.description: The Regulation Limit is mapped as the greatest extent of: • 15m of criteria layers: Crest of slope, Meander Belt, Flood hazard engineered, Flood hazard Estimated, Shoreline Hazard • the Areas of Interference (30 metres) adjacent to all wetlands. The greatest extent of all features identified above is the Regulation Limit provided on the TRCA Regulation Limit mapping. It should be noted that compliance with this regulation does not exempt applicants from having regard for local by-laws, municipal and regional official plans (which incorporate provisions of the Oak Ridges Moraine Conservation Plan, the Growth Plan for the Greater Golden Horseshoe and the Greenbelt Plan), or the Provincial Policy Statement. TRCA’s Regulation mapping is a tool that conceptually shows the area of land within TRCA’s jurisdiction that is likely to be subject to the Regulation. The Regulation limit boundary is based on the best technical information available to TRCA at the time of the preparation of the map. Technical analysis that supports the mapping includes flood plain studies, provincial wetland mapping, ecological land classification mapping, digital elevation models, aerial photography, watercourse meander belt analysis, watercourse location mapping and Lake Ontario shoreline hazard assessment studies. </SPAN><SPAN>The jurisdiction-wide update was completed in 2006 as part of the Generic Regulation conformity exercise. The 2019 comprehensive update to the existing mapping has been undertaken to reflect new technical information on current aerial photography. The 2024 update to the existing mapping has been undertaken to reflect new technical information on current aerial photography. TRCA is following the guidance provided by Conservation Ontario for regulation mapping updates.

results.description:
This dataset shows normalized flood risk for all census tracts within the contiguous United States, as based on the First Street Foundation Flood Model. The normalization process takes the percentage of properties within a tract with exposure to the 100-year flood, and transforms this number to a percentile (relative to all other census tracts).
 
First Street Foundation is a non-profit research and technology group defining America’s flood risk. Please let us know how your organization is using our publicly available data offered through ArcGIS Online (e.g. resiliency reports, adaptation studies, etc.). This helps inform what datasets we make publicly available in the future. Contact datashare@firststreet.org.
 
First Street Foundation is committed to the accuracy of the data and will continue to grow, adapt, and change the Flood Model with new and better information. As such, improvements to the Flood Model are incorporated in quarterly updates. The statistics presented here are consistent with First Street Foundation Flood Model version 1.3 released on May 7, 2021.
 
The aggregated data presented here are available from First Street Foundation at the individual property level. Please go to First Street’s Data Access page for more information.

Dataset Field Names

The following fields are included in this dataset:

Attribute

Description

FIPS

Census Tract FIPS Code

COUNTY

County

STATE

State

norm_2020

Normalized flood risk percentile for the year 2020. Based on percent of properties within the census tract with exposure to the 100 year flood in the medium climate scenario. Percentile relative to all other tracts in the contiguous United States.

norm_2050

Normalized flood risk percentile for the year 2050. Based on percent of properties within the census tract with exposure to the 100 year flood in the medium climate scenario. Percentile relative to all other tracts in the contiguous United States.

diff_2020_2050

Percentile difference between “norm_2020” and “norm_2050”. This number will be positive for tracts that are projected to increase in flood risk relative to other tracts over the next 30 years. This number will be negative for tracts that are projected to decrease in flood risk relative to other tracts over the next 30 years.


Normalization Method

The method used to normalize flood risk is based on a min-max scaling process that assigns a percentile to each census tract in the contiguous United States. The percentile is based on percent of properties within the tract with exposure to the 100 year flood in the medium climate scenario (the First Street Foundation Flood Model incorporates the output of an ensemble of 21 Global Climate Models to account for the uncertainty of future climate scenarios as well as the current climate itself).

The min-max scaling method results in a transformation to percentiles within a range of values that are restricted to the minimum and maximum values of the variable being scaled. The equation is (value - min) / (max - min), where each term represents the following:
  • value: the % of properties exposed to the hazard in each specific year
  • min: the minimum % of properties exposed to the hazard in each specific year
  • max: the maximum % of properties exposed to the hazard in each specific year
First Street Data Availability

The aggregated data presented here are available from First Street Foundation at the individual property level. Please go to First Street’s Data Access page for more information.

results.title: Potential Storm Surge Flooding (NOAA)
results.description:
Last Revised: August 2016
Map Information

This nowCOAST™ map service provides maps depicting the latest official NWS Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map for any significant landfalling tropical cyclone expected to impact the Atlantic or Gulf of Mexico Coasts of the Contiguous United States. The map layers depict the risk associated with coastal flooding from storm surge associated with tropical cyclones.

The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map depicts the geographical areas where inundation from storm surge could occur along with the heights, above ground, that water could reach in those areas. These potential heights are represented with different colors based on water level: 1) Greater than 1 foot above ground (blue), 2) Greater than 3 feet above ground (yellow), 3) Greater than 6 feet above ground (orange), and 4) Greater than 9 feet above ground (red). Two versions of this graphic are provided in this map--one with a mask (depicted in gray) identifying Intertidal Zone/Estuarine Wetland areas, and another version without the mask where Intertidal Zone/Estuarine Wetland areas are symbolized with the same colors as other areas.

Two additional layers are provided to depict 1) the full geographic extent for which the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map is presently valid (the "map boundary"), and 2) Levee Areas, if any, within the affected area (symbolized with a black-and-white diagonal hatch pattern).

If the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map is not presently active, all layers will be blank except for the Map Boundary layer, which will display a shaded region indicating the coverage area for any potential future graphics along with a text label indicating that the map is not presently available.

This map service is updated approximately every 10 minutes on nowCOAST™ to ensure the latest information is provided to the user as soon as it becomes available. Once issued, the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map will be updated by NHC every six hours alongside each new Forecast Advisory for the associated tropical cyclone. However, due to processing requirements during the creation of this product, the flooding map becomes available approximately 60 to 90 minutes following the release of the associated NHC Forecast Advisory, at which point nowCOAST™ will acquire it and update this map service within the next 10 to 20 minutes (i.e., this product will be updated on nowCOAST™ within approximately 70 to 110 minutes after the associated Forecast Advisory is released). For more detailed information about layer update frequency and timing, please reference the nowCOAST™ Dataset Update Schedule.

Background Information

Developed by National Hurricane Center (NHC) over the course of several years in consultation with social scientists, emergency managers, broadcast meteorologists, and others, the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map is intended to depict the risk associated with coastal flooding from storm surge associated with tropical cyclones. On June 1, 2016 it became an operational product, issued on demand for certain tropical cyclones that are expected to affect the Atlantic and Gulf Coasts of the United States. The product is not available for tropical cyclones that may affect coastal areas in the Eastern or Central Pacific regions.

From the NHC Website:

"What the Map Takes into Account

The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map is based on the NWS Sea, Lake, and Overland Surges from Hurricanes (SLOSH) model and takes into account forecast uncertainty in the tropical cyclone track, intensity, and wind field. The map is based on probabilistic storm surge guidance developed by the NWS Meteorological Development Laboratory (MDL), in cooperation with NHC, called Probabilistic Hurricane Storm Surge (P-Surge 2.5).

P-Surge 2.5 derives storm surge probabilities by statistically evaluating a large set of SLOSH model simulations based on the current NHC official forecast, and takes into account historical errors in the official NHC track and intensity forecasts. P-Surge 2.5 combines the results of hundreds of individual SLOSH simulations to calculate the statistical distribution, or probabilities of possible storm surge heights at locations along the coast. All major factors that influence the amount of storm surge generated by a storm at a given location are accounted for, including the hurricane's landfall location, forward speed, and angle of approach to the coast; the storm intensity and wind field; the shape of the coastline; the slope of the ocean bottom; and local features such as barrier islands, bays, and rivers. The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map is created by processing the resulting 10 percent exceedance levels from P-Surge 2.5, or storm surge values that have a 1-in-10 chance of being exceeded at each location.

The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map takes into account:

  • Flooding due to storm surge from the ocean, including adjoining tidal rivers, sounds, and bays
  • Normal astronomical tides
  • Land elevation
  • Uncertainties in the landfall location, forward speed, angle of approach to the coast, intensity, and wind field of the cyclone

The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map does not take into account:

  • Wave action
  • Freshwater flooding from rainfall
  • Flooding resulting from levee failures
  • For mapped leveed areas - flooding inside levees, overtopping of levees

Potential storm surge flooding is not depicted within certain levee areas, such as the Hurricane & Storm Damage Risk Reduction System in Louisiana. These areas are highly complex and water levels resulting from overtopping are difficult to predict. Users are urged to consult local officials for flood risk inside these leveed areas. If applicable to the region displayed by the map, these leveed areas will be depicted with a black and white diagonal hatch pattern.

The intertidal zone, or generally speaking, the area that is above water at low tide and under water at high tide, will be displayed with a user selectable mask layer on the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map. Locations of estuarine wetlands, or lands that are saturated with water, either permanently or seasonally, are also used to help define this mask layer. This mask layer will allow users to differentiate between areas that could experience consequential flooding of normally dry ground and areas that routinely flood during typical high tides. The intertidal mask will be depicted as gray on the Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map.

What the Map Represents

The Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map represents the storm surge heights that a person should prepare for before a storm, given the uncertainties in the meteorological forecast. The map shows a reasonable worst-case scenario (i.e., a reasonable upper bound) of the flooding of normally dry land at particular locations due to storm surge. There is approximately a 1-in-10 chance that storm surge flooding at any particular location could be higher than the values shown on the map. Roadways are included in the basemap layer for aiding in geographical referencing only. The map will not indicate which roadways may flood from fresh or salt water in a hurricane situation."

For more information about the NHC Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map, please consult the NHC Website or the associated NWS Product Description Document (PDD).

Time Information

This nowCOAST™ map service is not time-enabled.

  • NWS, 2016: Potential Storm Surge Flooding Map Product Description Document, NWS, Silver Spring, MD (Available at http://www.nhc.noaa.gov/pdf/PDD-PotentialStormSurgeFloodingMap.pdf).
